qc_c_ligne_jaune_10_000_zoulous.blurb: This wall is one of the sectors at Weir in the Laurentians, and it is the first cliff you meet when you set off up the trail from the parking area. It holds 21 routes, 14 of them bolted sport lines and 7 trad lines, a few of which go on for several pitches. Difficulty sits high: most climbs fall in the 5.11 and 5.12 range, a handful reach 5.13, and only a few are 5.10 or easier, so it suits climbers already working at a harder level. Expect poison ivy near the path and the occasional loose block.

qc_le_parapluie.blurb: A steep, well-regarded cliff in Chicoutimi, part of the La Croix climbing area in the Saguenay region and reached by a short path that drops down from a city park. Most of its 21 routes are bolted sport lines, with several trad lines and a single aid route mixed in. The standard is demanding: grades start around 5.7 and reach into 5.14, but the bulk of the climbs sit between 5.11 and 5.13, and easy lines are scarce. It is regarded as a destination for strong climbers looking for hard sport and trad on one wall.

qc_cap_des_couleurs.blurb: A compact school crag inside a municipal park in Rouyn-Noranda, in the Abitibi-Témiscamingue region, put together by local volunteers as a friendly place to learn and to bring family. The wall stands only a few steps from the car. Of its 21 routes, about half are bolted sport lines and most of the others are trad, plus one top-rope line and one hard boulder problem. Grades are gentle: the great majority run from around 5.2 to 5.9, with just one at 5.10, which makes it a sensible choice for beginners, instructors and relaxed days out.

qc_tranchant_right.blurb: The right-hand sector of Montagne du Tranchant, a busy cliff in Lanaudière near Saint-Côme, and the part of the cliff where the harder lines are found. Its 21 routes are mostly bolted sport climbs, with three trad lines. Grades run from 5.8 up to 5.13, though most sit in the 5.10 to 5.12 band and 5.12 is the most common. Many routes begin from a raised ledge, so a fall low down can be serious, and some first bolts are placed so you can stick-clip them. Lines here can stay damp for a long time in spring.

qc_paroi_l_phant.blurb: A west-facing granite cliff that rises straight out of the water in Parc régional du Poisson Blanc, in the Laurentians. The wall is roughly 30 to 35 m tall and very wide. It is a remote destination: you get there by boat or a long paddle, and a boat is needed to belay from the base. Climbs mix sport, trad and top-rope, mostly from about 5.5 to 5.12, with the largest group at 5.10 and 5.11. A trail leads up to the top for anchors, and backcountry campsites a short paddle away make a handy base.

qc_cap_trinit.blurb: A big cliff above the Saguenay fjord in Parc national du Fjord-du-Saguenay, close to Rivière-Éternité. Routes are long, roughly 150 to 300 m, and follow crack systems; around half of the 20 listed climbs are aid and the rest are trad. Free climbing is mostly very hard, in the 5.12 and 5.13 range, with a few moderate options between 5.8 and 5.10. The rock is a mix of strong grey granite and flaky orange stone. It is rarely crowded and can be windy. Reaching the base means a boat, a paddle or a steep bushwhacking hike.
